title: Puppy Teething: Timeline, Signs and Safe Things to Chew
description: When puppies lose baby teeth, what teething looks like, and which chews are safe. A clear timeline for new owners.

quick: Puppies have about 28 baby teeth. They start losing them at roughly 12 to 16 weeks, and by about 6 months most have their adult set of about 42 teeth. During that time, offer safe chew toys and soft chews. Avoid bones, rawhide and anything too hard to dent with a fingernail, and ask your vet to check your puppy's mouth.

faq.a: Baby teeth start to come in at around 2 to 4 weeks, while the puppy is still with the breeder. The second round, when baby teeth fall out and adult teeth push through, usually starts at around 12 to 16 weeks, according to the American Kennel Club.

faq.q: How long does puppy teething last?
faq.a: Most puppies have lost all their baby teeth and grown their adult teeth by about 6 months. The exact timing varies, so ask your vet to check your puppy's mouth if baby teeth are still in place after that.

faq.q: Are bones, antlers or rawhide safe for teething puppies?
faq.a: PDSA says bones are not a good chew because they can break teeth or splinter and pierce the gut, and it does not recommend rawhide because it can splinter. Its test for chew treats is that they should be soft enough to dent with your fingernail. If you are unsure about a specific chew, ask your vet.

faq.q: Why is my puppy biting so much while teething?
faq.a: Sore gums make firm things attractive, and your hands and clothes are within reach. Redirect to a suitable chew toy and read our guide to how to stop puppy biting.

html:
One morning you find a tiny, rice-sized tooth on the carpet. Your puppy is gnawing the table leg, and your hands look like they have been through a rose bush. Welcome to teething. It is a normal stage, it does not last forever, and you can make it a lot easier on everyone.

Puppy teething timeline

Puppies, like human babies, grow two sets of teeth. This timeline follows the American Kennel Club's guide. Your puppy may be a little earlier or later, and your vet can check how things are going.

AgeWhat is happeningWhat helps
2 to 4 weeksBaby teeth begin to come in, while the puppy is still with the mother and breederNothing for you to do yet
5 to 6 weeksAll the baby teeth should be in, about 28 in totalBreeder is weaning onto soft food
12 to 16 weeksBaby teeth start to fall out and adult teeth emerge. You may find tiny teeth around the houseSafe chew toys, a vet check of the mouth, gentle touching of the mouth
About 6 monthsBaby teeth should all be gone, and adult dogs have about 42 teethTell your vet if any baby teeth remain

Signs your puppy is teething

Teething does not look the same in every puppy, but these are common. Your puppy chews on more things than usual, including your hands. The gums look a little red. You may spot small teeth on the floor or in toys. Some puppies are a bit fussier than normal, and some eat less comfortably for a few days.

If your puppy refuses food for more than a day, has bleeding that does not stop, a swollen face, or very bad breath, call your vet instead of assuming it is teething.

What can a teething puppy safely chew?

The AKC says to offer safe chew toys from around 12 to 16 weeks. PDSA gives a very practical test for chew treats and toys: they should be soft enough that you can dent them with your fingernail, because if they are too hard they can damage teeth and gums. PDSA also says to rotate toys so your puppy does not get bored.

  • Rubber toys with some give, sized so they cannot be swallowed.
  • Soft textured toys made for puppies, checked often for damage.
  • Chews recommended by your vet for your puppy's age and size.

Are bones, antlers and rawhide safe?

This is one of the most searched questions, and the cautious answer is to skip them. PDSA says bones are not a good chew treat, because they can break teeth, or splinter in the stomach and pierce the gut. They can also cause constipation, or a blockage if large pieces are swallowed. PDSA also does not recommend rawhide, as it can splinter and potentially hurt your dog. Antlers and other very hard chews fail the fingernail test, so they carry the same risk to teeth that are still growing. Whatever you choose, check with your vet, and supervise.

How to ease teething at home

  1. Keep several toys within reach and swap them every day or two.
  2. Redirect, do not scold. When teeth touch skin, calmly pause, then offer a toy and praise when it is chewed. Our pause, redirect, reward method shows how.
  3. Puppy-proof cables, shoes and table legs, or block access with a pen or gate.
  4. Handle the mouth gently for a few seconds a day with a treat, so a later vet check or tooth brushing is easier.
  5. Plan chew time when your puppy is tired and cranky. Overtired puppies bite more.

When to ask the vet

Ask your vet to look at your puppy's mouth around the time the baby teeth start to fall, and tell your vet if any baby teeth are still there at around 6 months, as the AKC advises. Also call the vet if your puppy has a broken tooth, bleeding gums, drools heavily, cries when eating, or seems unwell. Teething is not usually a medical problem, but a vet can tell the difference.

The biting that comes with teething usually settles as the adult teeth arrive. For the longer picture, read when does puppy biting stop.
